summary: Defines a metadata format that an OAuth 2.0 client or authorization server can use to learn what it needs to interact with a protected resource.

eli5.summary: A service publishes an info sheet that says how to talk to it and which login service to use, so apps can set up automatically.

questions: how does an oauth client discover a resource server
what is oauth protected resource metadata
how does a client find the authorization server for an api
subtitle: A standard JSON document that tells OAuth clients how a protected API works and which authorization server to use.

tldr.problem: An OAuth 2.0 client that meets a protected resource it has never seen needs to learn its requirements, such as which scopes exist, how to send a token and which authorization server issues tokens for it.
tldr.mechanism: The resource publishes a JSON metadata document at a well-known URL derived from its resource identifier, by default /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource. It can also point clients to it with a resource_metadata parameter in a WWW-Authenticate response.
tldr.outcome: Clients and authorization servers can set themselves up automatically, and a resource server can change its authorization servers without other coordination with clients. The client must check that the returned resource value matches the identifier it used.

today: RFC 9728 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to sit alongside RFC 8414 and RFC 7591, which it deliberately parallels.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
This specification defines a metadata format that OAuth 2.0 clients and authorization servers can use to learn what they need to interact with a protected resource. It is intentionally parallel in structure to RFC 7591 (Dynamic Client Registration), where a client gives metadata about itself, and RFC 8414 (Authorization Server Metadata), where a client learns about an authorization server.

How a client finds the location of the protected resource is out of scope. It might be configured by hand, such as a user typing the URL of a JMAP server into an email client, or discovered dynamically, for example through WebFinger.

The RFC defines one term, the Resource Identifier: the protected resource's URL, which uses the https scheme and has no fragment. It SHOULD NOT include a query component, though some cases need one. The metadata is published at a well-known location derived from this identifier, so that each resource has its own deterministic metadata address. This is what stops an attacker from publishing metadata that claims to describe a resource it does not control.
sections.eli5: An app that meets a new service needs to know the rules. The service writes its rules on a sheet kept at an address that anyone can work out from the service's own name.

sections.title: Metadata Parameters
sections.content:
The only REQUIRED parameter is resource, the resource identifier. scopes_supported and resource_name are RECOMMENDED. The rest are OPTIONAL, including:

  • authorization_servers: a JSON array of issuer identifiers for authorization servers usable with the resource. A resource may choose not to advertise some of them.
  • jwks_uri: an https URL of the resource's JSON Web Key Set, for example keys used to sign resource responses.
  • bearer_methods_supported: the ways to send a bearer token, with defined values header, body and query.
  • resource_signing_alg_values_supported: supported signing algorithms; the value none MUST NOT be used.
  • resource_documentation, resource_policy_uri and resource_tos_uri: human-readable pages.
  • tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens, dpop_signing_alg_values_supported, dpop_bound_access_tokens_required and authorization_details_types_supported: support for certificate-bound tokens, DPoP and rich authorization requests.

Additional parameters MAY be used. Human-readable values can be given in several languages by adding a language tag after a hash sign, for example resource_name#it. A metadata value may also be supplied as signed_metadata, a JWT containing the metadata as claims. It MUST be signed or MACed and MUST contain an iss claim. A consumer that supports signed metadata MUST give its values precedence over plain JSON values, but consumers MAY ignore it.
sections.eli5: The sheet has a name, a list of the passes you can ask for, and which office to visit. It can be written in several languages, and it can carry a signature to show who vouches for it.

sections.title: Fetching and Validating the Metadata
sections.content:
The metadata URL is formed by inserting a well-known string between the host and the path and/or query of the resource identifier. By default the string is /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource. For https://resource.example.com the request is GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource; for https://resource.example.com/resource1 it is GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/resource1. Any terminating slash after the host is removed before insertion. Using the path this way lets one host serve several resources, which some multi-tenant setups require.

A successful response MUST be 200 OK with the application/json content type. Unknown parameters MUST be ignored, and parameters with zero values MUST be omitted. Applications may register their own well-known suffix, but general-purpose resources use the default.

Validation matters. The returned resource value MUST be identical to the resource identifier used to build the URL. If the metadata came from a URL given in a WWW-Authenticate challenge, resource MUST be identical to the URL the client used to request the resource. If they differ, the data MUST NOT be used. A signed metadata signature must be verified, and an invalid signature or untrusted issuer SHOULD be treated as an error. String comparisons are code point to code point, with no Unicode normalization.
sections.eli5: The app builds the sheet's address from the service's name, then checks the sheet really names that same service. If the names do not match, it throws the sheet away.

sections.title: WWW-Authenticate and Authorization Server Metadata
sections.content:
A resource server MAY return the metadata URL in a WWW-Authenticate response header, using the new resource_metadata parameter. The RFC's example is a 401 Unauthorized with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://resource.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource". The parameter may be used with other schemes such as DPoP. A resource may send such a challenge at any time to signal that its metadata may have changed, and the client SHOULD then retrieve and validate the new metadata. This lets a resource server change its authorization servers with no other coordination with clients.

The RFC also adds one authorization server metadata parameter, protected_resources, a list of resource identifiers usable with that server. When both lists can be enumerated, the two sides should be cross-checked for consistency. The way a client gets its client identifier is out of scope; Dynamic Client Registration is given as one existing method. Resource servers MAY also return other WWW-Authenticate headers, so clients that do not implement this specification can still choose another scheme.
sections.eli5: When a guard turns an app away, he can hand over a note saying where the information sheet is. If the rules change, he can hand over the note again.

sections.title: The End-to-End Flow
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the authorization code flow, noting that other OAuth flows work similarly. The client first asks for the resource without an access token. The resource server answers with a WWW-Authenticate header that carries the metadata URL. The client fetches and validates the metadata, then builds the authorization server metadata URL from an issuer identifier in it, following RFC 8414, and fetches that metadata.

The client then sends the user to the authorization server, completes the authorization exchange and obtains an access token. Finally it repeats the original request with the token and the resource server returns the resource.
sections.eli5: The app knocks, gets told to read the sheet, reads it, goes to the right office for a pass, then comes back with the pass and is let in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support TLS and follow BCP 195. Clients MUST check the server certificate when fetching metadata, which defends against adversary-in-the-middle and DNS-based attacks that could trick a client into using an attacker's resource server. Matching the resource value to the identifier, as in the validation step, defends against an attacker publishing a document that claims another resource's identifier.

  • Scopes: scopes_supported lists what the server will disclose, and the client should still request as limited a scope as possible.
  • Audience restriction: a client that talks to several resource servers SHOULD request audience-restricted tokens using RFC 8707. Without them, a malicious resource server could get a client to obtain a token for another server and reuse it there.
  • SSRF: because clients fetch metadata from servers they do not know, they SHOULD guard against Server-Side Request Forgery, for example by blocking requests to internal IP address ranges.
  • Phishing: a malicious or compromised user-selected resource could mislead users. Clear notice and showing the authorization server's domain name reduce the risk but do not eliminate it.
  • Signed versus unsigned: unsigned metadata depends on TLS and the Internet PKI, while signed metadata is also protected by the issuer's signature.
  • Caching: normal HTTP caching applies, and implementations should use directives such as Cache-Control with max-age.

The RFC states that secure determination of the right authorization servers for a resource is out of scope. An inappropriate authorization server could let an attacker act as an adversary-in-the-middle.
sections.eli5: The app must make sure the sheet really belongs to the service, ask for only the pass it needs, and be careful not to be tricked into visiting places it should not.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC establishes the "OAuth Protected Resource Metadata" registry, whose entries record a metadata name and the specification that defines it. Values are registered through Specification Required, with review by designated experts, who should check that a name is unique, generally applicable and clear. Requests are sent to a review mailing list. The initial contents are the parameters defined in Section 2 of the RFC.

It also registers protected_resources in the OAuth Authorization Server Metadata registry and adds an entry to the Well-Known URIs registry for the default suffix.
sections.eli5: There is an official notebook of every allowed entry for the sheet, and a small group of reviewers checks new entries before they go in.
